FACTS.identity: Name: Li Zhiqiang (fictional teaching patient). Male, 46 years old, married, warehouse management employee. History provided by the patient and spouse; reliable. Department: general orthopedic outpatient clinic; not yet admitted. No real identity, address, phone number, or hospital identifier.
FACTS.pain: Lower back pain with radiating pain in the left lower limb for 8 weeks, worsening with left foot dorsiflexion weakness for 2 days. Lower back pain began on July 9, 2026, after bending over to move boxes. The following day, radiating pain and numbness developed in the left buttock, posterolateral thigh, lateral lower leg, dorsum of the foot, and first toe web space. Symptoms worsen with coughing, sneezing, prolonged sitting, and bending, and improve when lying on the side with the hips and knees flexed. Initially, lower back pain was NRS 4/10 and leg pain 6/10; currently, leg pain is 8/10 and lower back pain 4/10. He needs to stop after walking approximately 100 meters and wakes at night because of pain. Bilateral intermittent claudication is not the predominant symptom. Since September 1, he has had difficulty lifting the left foot, with the toes tending to catch on the ground. This worsened on September 2, and he cannot walk on the left heel alone.
FACTS.previous: After symptom onset, approximately 8 weeks of outpatient nonsurgical treatment were provided for suspected lumbar disc herniation, including a short course of celecoxib 200 mg once daily, acetaminophen as needed, rehabilitation exercises that did not provoke leg pain, and modifications to lifting and prolonged sitting. NSAIDs were not used continuously for the full 8 weeks. Pain recurred after temporary relief, and work and sleep remained substantially impaired. No lumbar injections or previous surgery. The outpatient record dated 2026-08-28 documented left great toe dorsiflexion of 4/5, with other major muscle groups at 5/5. Imaging was performed to assess bony structures and stability.
FACTS.negatives: No urinary retention, urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence, perineal numbness, or new sexual dysfunction; no simultaneous weakness of both lower limbs. No fever, chills, progressively worsening nighttime pain at rest, or unexplained weight loss; no history of malignancy, immunosuppression, intravenous drug abuse, or recent infection. No major trauma or long-term steroid use. Appetite is fair; recent sleep has been affected by pain. Bladder and bowel function are normal.
FACTS.past: Denies a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, stroke, chronic kidney disease, or gastrointestinal ulcer bleeding. No history of spinal surgery, anesthesia-related adverse events, bleeding disorders, or venous thrombosis. No long-term anticoagulant or antiplatelet use.
FACTS.allergy: Intermittent celecoxib use at 200 mg/day over the past week, most recently on 2026-09-02; occasional acetaminophen use. Denies known drug, latex, or contrast agent allergies. All imaging is specified as noncontrast, with no contrast exposure.
FACTS.social: Smoking history approximately 15 pack-years, averaging 10 cigarettes/day in recent years; occasional alcohol use. Work involves prolonged alternating sitting and standing, with frequent heavy lifting in the past. Married with one daughter and good family support. No family history of spinal deformities or hereditary neuromuscular disorders.
FACTS.ward_patient: Postoperative day 1: left leg pain 1–2/10, reduced numbness over the dorsum of the foot, able to walk with support, and normal spontaneous urination.
FACTS.discharge_patient: Leg pain 1/10, mild residual numbness over the dorsum of the foot, able to walk with protection, and normal bladder and bowel function.
FACTS.prior_episodes: During the two or three years before this episode, he occasionally experienced aching and a sense of fullness in the lower back after moving many items, bending to organize goods, or a busy day, approximately two or three times a year, though he cannot recall the exact frequency. It usually resolved after one or two days of rest, after which he could work as usual. Previously, there was only low back aching and fullness, without pain extending from the left buttock down to the lower leg and top of the foot as in this episode, and without foot numbness, difficulty lifting the foot, or tripping while walking. He did not seek specific medical care, undergo imaging, or receive prescription treatment for those brief episodes of low back aching, and had not been diagnosed with lumbar disc herniation. The similarity to this episode is low back discomfort, but previous episodes did not involve the current persistent radiating leg pain and weakness. This episode began with persistent pain after moving boxes on July 9, followed by radiating left leg pain and numbness the next day; difficulty lifting the foot did not appear until September 1. The previous occasional low back aching must not be counted as part of the duration of this persistent episode.
FACTS.daily_life: Originally from Pidu District, Chengdu; has worked and lived in Chengdu since starting a family and currently lives in Wuhou District. Refer to the outpatient registration for the detailed address. Married, living with his wife and one daughter; his wife knows about the current low back and leg symptoms and accompanied him to the visit. Has worked in warehouse management for over ten years, usually checking inventory, recording incoming and outgoing stock, and inspecting the warehouse, sometimes helping move boxes. His work involves both sitting to enter records and standing or walking, rather than sitting in an office all day. After work, he enjoys watching the news and chatting with his family. Before the onset of his low back and leg symptoms, he would walk around his residential complex; he has no regular high-intensity exercise routine. Recent pain has affected his work and sleep. His main concern is that difficulty lifting his foot may affect future walking and work, and he wants to understand how treatment may help recovery; this does not mean he has agreed to or refused any particular treatment. He came to this hospital because an acquaintance said its orthopedic care was good, and he also wants to understand why this episode has not improved; do not invent appointments, referrals, travel times, or prehospital treatment. He may generally be addressed as Mr. Li. He is unfamiliar with medical terminology and describes his symptoms in everyday terms such as an aching lower back, pulling pain in the leg, numbness on the top of the foot, and difficulty lifting the foot.

exam.text:
T 36.6°C, P 78 beats/min, R 18 breaths/min, BP 128/78 mmHg, SpO₂ 98%. Height 176 cm, weight 78 kg, BMI 25.2 kg/m². Alert, with a pained expression; no significant abnormalities on cardiac, pulmonary, or abdominal examination. No lower-extremity swelling; dorsalis pedis pulses are symmetric.
Mild rightward trunk shift when standing, with limited lumbar forward flexion; left-sided paraspinal tenderness at L4/5, with no significant bony pain on percussion. Left straight leg raising at 35° elicited typical ipsilateral radiating pain, with a positive ankle dorsiflexion augmentation test. ct.name: Noncontrast lumbar spine CT with coronal and sagittal 2D reconstructions
ct.text:
The specified scan range extends from the inferior margin of T12 to S2, using thin-section noncontrast imaging with coronal and sagittal reconstructions. A left-sided soft-tissue density is visible at the posterior margin of L4/5, with narrowing of the left lateral recess. No obvious extensive calcification of the nucleus pulposus is seen; the cortical bone of the vertebral bodies, pedicles, and pars interarticularis is intact. Mild facet degeneration, without definite spondylolysis, severe bony spinal canal stenosis, or fracture.
 Imaging impression：Possible left posterolateral L4/5 disc herniation; MRI is recommended to assess nerve roots and soft tissues. No definite bony contraindication to surgery or indication for fixation.

mr.name: Lumbar spine MRI Noncontrast scan
mr.text:
Teaching sequence setup: sagittal T1WI and T2WI, and axial T2WI covering the inferior border of T12 to S2. The actual MRI coverage and axial angulation must be determined according to clinical protocols. The conus medullaris terminates at approximately L1, with no definite signal abnormality. The L4/5 disc shows decreased T2 signal and mild disc space narrowing. A left paracentral/lateral recess nucleus pulposus extrusion with slight caudal migration compresses the left anterior margin of the thecal sac and the traversing left L5 nerve root. The causative lesion is not an extraforaminal L4/5 disc herniation, nor is compression of the exiting left L4 nerve root the predominant finding. There is a mild L5/S1 disc bulge without definite corresponding nerve root compression; no major compressive lesion is seen at the other levels. No major findings support infection, tumor, or acute fracture.
 Imaging impression：Left-sided extruded lumbar disc herniation at L4/5, with caudal migration and compression of the left L5 nerve root, consistent with the physical findings. Confirm morphology, level, and laterality using the original imaging data; the current image is AI-generated for teaching and lacks diagnostic-grade spatial consistency.

handoff.name: Surgical team report
handoff.text:
After induction of general anesthesia, the patient was positioned prone with the abdomen free. L4/5 was localized fluoroscopically, and the level and left side were verified. Cefazolin 2 g was administered intravenously for prophylaxis 30 minutes before skin incision. A short left-sided incision and limited paraspinal muscle dissection were performed, followed by a limited interlaminar fenestration under the microscope, preserving sufficient facet joint tissue. The left L5 nerve root was exposed, revealing ventral compression by extruded nucleus pulposus. Extruded and loose nucleus pulposus fragments were removed, avoiding excessive disc curettage. Exploration confirmed nerve root decompression and restoration of thecal sac pulsation. Hemostasis was achieved, with no cerebrospinal fluid leak observed. No internal fixation or fusion was performed. Estimated blood loss was 30 mL. The procedure was uneventful, with no transfusion. Synthetic pathology conclusion for the submitted specimen: degenerative fibrocartilage/nucleus pulposus tissue.
Alert, with stable vital signs; left leg pain decreased to 2/10 and incision pain is 3/10. Left ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension remain 3/5, sensory loss persists, and the toes are warm. No new perineal numbness or difficulty urinating, and no significant incisional bleeding. Short-term analgesia, neurological examinations, mechanical prophylaxis, and early mobilization; no routine repeat CT/MRI without an abnormal finding warranting it.

ward.text: Left leg pain is 1–2/10; left ankle and great toe dorsiflexion have improved to 4/5, with reduced numbness over the dorsum of the foot. Stop prophylactic antibiotics within 24 hours after surgery; reassess venous thrombosis prevention based on mobility, bleeding, and individual risk.

handoff.name: Surgical team report
handoff.text:
After induction of general anesthesia, the patient was positioned prone with the abdomen free. L4/5 was localized fluoroscopically, and the level and left side were verified. Cefazolin 2 g was administered intravenously for prophylaxis 30 minutes before skin incision. A short left-sided incision and limited paraspinal muscle dissection were performed, followed by a limited interlaminar fenestration under the microscope, preserving sufficient facet joint tissue. The left L5 nerve root was exposed, revealing ventral compression by extruded nucleus pulposus. Extruded and loose nucleus pulposus fragments were removed, avoiding excessive disc curettage. Exploration confirmed nerve root decompression and restoration of thecal sac pulsation. Hemostasis was achieved, with no cerebrospinal fluid leak observed. No internal fixation or fusion was performed. Estimated blood loss was 30 mL. The procedure was uneventful, with no transfusion. Synthetic pathology conclusion for the submitted specimen: degenerative fibrocartilage/nucleus pulposus tissue.
Alert, with stable vital signs; left leg pain decreased to 2/10 and incision pain is 3/10. Left ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension remain 3/5, sensory loss persists, and the toes are warm. No new perineal numbness or difficulty urinating, and no significant incisional bleeding. Short-term analgesia, neurological examinations, mechanical prophylaxis, and early mobilization; no routine repeat CT/MRI without an abnormal finding warranting it.
